transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14 15:00 UTC / Duration: 56m
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Lead ML Eng, Pacific Dataworks), Maya Singh (Platform Eng), Carlos Ortega (CTO)

[00:00] Laura (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — dig into your prefix cache hit profile, talk tenant isolation options, go over quantization bench plans, and decide next steps for the on-prem pilot. Samir, you want to kick off with the cache recap?

[00:18] Samir (SE): Yeah, thanks. So just to set context, Redwood's default approach is per-tenant namespace prefixing before any shared KV store. That means keys are hashed as tenant_id + salt + prefix_hash, which gives us isolation but also affects hit locality. We commonly see a 2x difference in hit-rate if you omit tenant scoping when hotsets overlap.

[00:42] Jordan (PDW): Quick note — our workload is multi-tenant but with heavy skew: 30% of traffic from two enterprise tenants, long-tail from many small teams. We already bucket prompts by product line, but the prefix distribution is weird — many small prompts change a lot.

[01:05] Maya (PDW): And we must avoid any chance of prompt leakage between tenants — compliance requirement from our legal team. SOC2 plus some EU data residency rules.

[01:18] Samir (SE): Understood. So for strict isolation we recommend either tenant-prefixed keys or deterministic keyed hashing with a per-tenant salt stored in your KMS, rotated periodically. Advantages: even when keys collide at the hash layer, the salt ensures different final cache keys. Downside: rotation means you invalidate cached prefixes across the board, so you'll see cold-start churn after rotation unless you adopt dual-write warmup.

[01:45] Carlos (CTO): What's the operational burden of per-tenant salt? We run in an air-gapped on-prem setup for some customers — how does KMS integration work there?

[02:00] Samir (SE): For Private/on-prem we support customer-managed KMS (HSM or local KMS) — Redwood's control plane can be restricted or on a private network. Salt would be pulled at runtime from your local KMS; we only store non-sensitive derived keys if you opt-in. In fully air-gapped mode we can ship a helper that stores salts locally and rotates on a schedule.

[02:27] Jordan: That sounds okay. Our bigger question is hit-rate: our ops team reported ~18% KV hit overall, which seems low. What knobs should we tune?

[02:40] Samir (SE): 18% overall is low, but depends on hotset skew and how you compute key granularity. Common mistakes: including timestamps or user-session ids in the key, or not normalizing prompts (whitespace, punctuation). Two immediate levers: normalize and canonicalize prompts before keying; increase prefix bucketing to capture common templates; and consider TTL tuning with LRU vs LFU.

[03:10] Jordan: We do include conversation ids in some keys for safety — maybe that was a mistake.

[03:18] Maya: Also we have a policy of per-tenant short TTL (60s) to avoid stale suggestions, but maybe that's too conservative.

[03:28] Samir: TTL tuning is workload-specific. For chat style with long contexts, prefix KV cache helps more for system/prompt templates — those have very high reuse. If you short TTL everything to 60s you lose reusability. Suggest measuring per-key reuse distribution: 95th percentile lifetime of keys.

[03:50] Laura (AE): Samir, can you explain the eviction policy tradeoffs you'd recommend for Pacific Dataworks?

[03:55] Samir: Sure. LRU gives good recency; LFU is better for long-lived templated prompts. For multi-tenant safety, combine tenant-aware caches with a global memory budget per-tenant, enforced by weight-based eviction. For example, allocate 40% of cache to top tenants, 60% shared among small tenants but capped per-tenant so a noisy tenant can't evict everyone.

[04:22] Carlos: How do you implement caps without hurting hit-rate? If we cap top tenant at 40% but it's source of 70% of hits, we might lose latency wins.

[04:31] Samir: It's a tradeoff — you can make caps dynamic based on steady-state traffic. Also consider a small fast tier (hotset) for the very top N keys with pinning, and a bigger backing store for the rest. Pinning reduces churn for heavy tenants.

[04:47] Jordan: Can we get an example config to test? Like a recommended per-tenant budget and pin thresholds?

[04:53] Samir: Yes — action item for us to share a starter config. We'll include a combined LRU+LFU heuristic and shard affinity recommendations.

[05:05] Maya: Let's talk consistent hashing and shard affinity — we need cache locality for GPU KV-backed caches, right?

[05:12] Samir: Correct. For big deployments we use consistent hashing to map keys to shards. Important to pin hot keys to specific shards to avoid cross-shard fetches. For multi-region, prefer sticky routing by tenant region to reduce inter-region latency. Also, be careful with rebalancing: when you add/remove nodes, consistent hashing reduces churn but you still get some cold misses. Consider gradual rolling rebalancing during low traffic windows.

[05:40] Jordan: Our pilot will run 8 nodes — we plan to use A100s for now but could shift to H100 if needed. What implications for KV latency?

[05:51] Samir: On A100s latency per KV lookup is dominated by network and host-to-GPU packaging if you pin cache on-GPU for KV. If you use an in-memory CPU cache layer fronting GPU KV, you'll see sub-1ms for CPU memcache hits and ~5-15ms for GPU-backed hits depending on batch size. Our guidance: keep very hot keys in CPU cache to reduce tail latency.

[06:17] Laura: Talk to us about batching windows — our app needs p95 < 120ms for interactive flows. What batching parameters make sense?

[06:25] Samir: For p95 120ms you need small batching windows (5-15ms) and continuous batching to pack similar sequence lengths. But smaller windows reduce batch size and throughput. We typically tune batcher to target p50 latency and allow p95SLO headroom. Also consider dynamic batching that opens larger windows when queue depth increases.

[06:45] Maya: Any tips to avoid quality regressions with aggressive quantization? We saw hallucinations at int4 in a quick internal test.

[06:53] Samir: Yes — quantization tradeoffs are key. int8 typically preserves quality for most LLMs with 1-3% metric delta on instruction-following tasks; int4 and AWQ can be hit-or-miss. Best practice: run a small eval suite that includes safety-sensitive prompts and your top-100 production prompts. Redwood's Optimize module can run those regressions and flag thresholds. For production pilot we recommend testing: fp16 baseline, int8 (fine), int4/awq with careful QA.

[07:20] Jordan: Can Redwood run the quantization bench on our hotset? We can anonymize and drop PII.

[07:26] Samir: Yes — we offered to run quantization profiles against your hotset as long as we agree on data handling. We'll need a scrubbed sample (7-day) and an eval prompt set. We'll run int8, int4, awq, and provide per-prompt quality deltas and latency/cost numbers.

[07:45] Carlos: On telemetry: for our on-prem pilot we cannot allow request traces leaving site. How intrusive is Redwood's telemetry for Optimize?

[07:53] Samir: For Private deployments you can opt out of telemetry and provide only aggregate metrics. For benchmark runs we can execute all tests on-prem and produce a local report; if you want Redwood to analyze off-site we'd require explicit consent. We also support sending only hashed key digests instead of full prompts for analytics.

[08:13] Laura: Switching to cache key design — Samir, what normalization steps do you recommend?

[08:18] Samir: Normalize whitespace, lowercase where possible, strip redundant punctuation, canonicalize named entity placeholders (e.g., replace customer names with <USER> tokens), and reduce numeric noise by bucketing numbers. Also consider template extraction: separate the static system prompt and dynamic user fill-ins, key on the static part for prefix cache hits.

[08:42] Maya: If we canonicalize aggressively, we worry about accidentally merging prompts that should be distinct for safety audits. Any guardrails?

[08:51] Samir: Keep a hash map of original->canonical with a small TTL so you can audit transformations. Also log canonicalization decisions (not content) to your audit logs so compliance teams can track when two prompts were merged. If needed, store canonicalization version with the cache key so you can roll back changes without invalidating everything.

[09:13] Jordan: How about key length and storage overhead? Our candidate keys are currently ~256 bytes after context; do we need to shorten?

[09:20] Samir: Shorten for storage efficiency — use a two-step: canonicalize then compute a strong keyed hash (SHA256 truncated to 16 bytes) plus tenant-salt. That gives fixed-length keys and avoids storing whole prompts in cache index. For debugging you can keep a separate index with sampled mappings.

[09:42] Laura: Let's touch fallback policies —— if a keyed cache miss occurs and Dedicated capacity is saturated, what's the fallback chain?

[09:50] Samir: Typical chain: try hot CPU cache -> GPU KV backend -> lower-cost model variant (quantized) -> remote hosted fallback (if allowed) -> degrade to cached response with TTL-based safe fallback. For compliance-sensitive tenants, we disable remote hosted fallbacks. We can also configure automatic throttles and circuit-breakers to protect tail latency.

[10:15] Carlos: Can we rate-limit per-tenant to avoid noisy neighbor effects?

[10:20] Samir: Yes — Redwood supports per-tenant quotas on QPS, concurrent requests, and token consumption. Combine quotas with cache caps and pinning for top tenants.

[10:33] Jordan: On the bench itself — what metrics will you provide?

[10:37] Samir: We'll provide: hit-rate per-tenant, per-prefix-level hit curves, latency p50/p90/p95 for hits and misses, throughput (QPS) at various batch sizes, GPU utilization, cost per 1M tokens across quant profiles, and quality delta per eval prompt. We'll include heatmaps of prefix reuse and suggestions for TTL and bucket thresholds.

[10:59] Maya: Please include sample configs for LRU+LFU combine and for pinning top keys.

[11:05] Samir: Will do. Also we'll attach a shim script to anonymize logs and produce the sample hotset.

[11:12] Laura: Any security doc we can point them to now?

[11:16] Samir: I'll share the security pack link — it includes KMS integration, audit log details, SOC2 artifacts, and on-prem deployment checklist. Link: redwood.co/security-pack (placeholder).

[11:30] Jordan: Regarding quantization, you mentioned AWQ — we've heard mixed things. What's Redwood's stance?

[11:36] Samir: AWQ can be very efficient for certain decoder-only models but it's highly model-dependent. For instruction-tuned LLMs AWQ sometimes introduces hallucination in edge cases. We treat AWQ as experimental in production; int8 is the pragmatic sweet spot today.

[11:55] Maya: For the on-prem pilot, if we want to test AWQ, can you run it but tag it experimental and ensure rollback options?

[12:01] Samir: Yes, we'll provide rollback configs and model variance thresholds so your pipeline can switch back automatically if metric drift exceeds X%.

[12:12] Laura: Let's talk costs — Carlos, do you want a quick cost/benefit of Dedicated vs self-managed?

[12:18] Carlos: Please. Our ops team wants predictable monthly with a cap; we don't want surprise cloud bills.

[12:24] Laura: Dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable commit pricing and Redwood handles runtime orchestration, updates, and fallbacks. Self-managed saves platform fees but increases ops overhead — you need to run model packaging, kernel tuning, and benchmarking in-house. For Pacific Dataworks with strict compliance, Dedicated Private could be a good middle ground: customer-managed hardware with Redwood-managed control plane inside your VPC.

[12:48] Samir: One more runtime tip: enable prefix-level early exit caching for common completions (e.g., canned replies) — store full completions with a signature and return them instantly on exact match. Very useful for forms/FAQ workloads.

[13:07] Jordan: How do we ensure the audit trail for cached completions? We must show when and what cached result was returned.

[13:13] Samir: We log cache decision metadata — key hash, tenant, hit/miss, time, and which cache tier served the response. No payloads are logged unless you opt-in. These logs can be exported to your SIEM.

[13:28] Maya: Any gotchas with multi-tenant eviction under burst traffic?

[13:33] Samir: Burst traffic from a single tenant can thrash shared cache unless caps/pinning are in place. Also watch out for prefix hotspotting from templated prompts triggered by product launches. For that, pre-warm caches during rollout windows.

[13:49] Laura: We should pick concrete next steps — agreed: Redwood runs quant benchmarks, PDW supplies hotset, and we schedule pilot kickoff. Anything else?

[13:58] Carlos: Also please share an ops playbook for rotation, salt management, and emergency rollback.

[14:06] Samir: We'll share the playbook and the starter cache config.

[14:12] Jordan: One small question: you mentioned dual-write warmup during salt rotation — can you explain that pattern?

[14:18] Samir: Sure — dual-write means during rotation we write entries under both old and new salts for a grace period. On reads we check new salt first then fall back to old. After warmup window and once hit-rate under new salt is sufficiently high, you retire the old salt. This reduces mass cold misses.

[14:40] Maya: That helps. How long is the warmup window typically?

[14:44] Samir: Depends on traffic — 24-72 hours usually. We'll recommend based on observed key lifetimes.

[14:52] Laura: Any final compliance notes?

[14:55] Samir: Remember to set data retention policies per-tenant and use KMS to manage salts and any PII. For EU tenants ensure region pinning and no hosted fallbacks.

[15:08] Jordan: Sounds good. We'll anonymize logs and upload by Friday.

[15:14] Maya: One last Q: can Redwood's Optimize recommend quantization per-model automatically?

[15:19] Samir: Yes — Optimize can scan eval results and recommend profiles per-model and per-workload. It can also suggest batching and cache TTL changes to hit cost/latency targets.

[15:32] Laura: Great. Quick recap of next steps — share bench sheet + config, customer shares hotset, run quant tests, schedule pilot kickoff. Anything else?

[15:42] Carlos: No, that's it. Thanks.

[15:45] Laura: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and DRI items.

[15:50] (call ends)
